title: Pathogen Inactivation Using Substrate Thymol and Carvacrol Pretreatment During Anaerobic Digestion
content:
Pretreatment of swine manure with the plant-derived compounds carvacrol and thymol enhanced the inactivation of Ascaris suum eggs during anaerobic digestion without significantly reducing methane production. Carvacrol was particularly effective, accelerating pathogen inactivation and supporting the potential of this approach for safer organic waste recycling.


ABSTRACT

Anaerobic digestion does not always ensure complete inactivation of helminth eggs in livestock manure. This laboratory-scale proof-of-concept study evaluated whether pretreatment of swine feces with the plant-derived monoterpenes thymol and carvacrol enhances the inactivation of naturally occurring Ascaris suum eggs during mesophilic anaerobic digestion. Feces (50 g; on average 1533 eggs/g) were pretreated for 24 h with 15 mL of a 0.1% aqueous thymol or carvacrol preparation (0.3 mg of active compound per g of fresh substrate) and digested in 1 L batch bioreactors at 37°Cfor 18 days, with two independent bioreactors per treatment; untreated feces served as the control. Samples collected every 3 days were incubated for 60 days at 28°C, and egg development (one-cell stage, cleavage, formed larva) was assessed. Methane concentration in the biogas (% v/v) was measured on days 6, 12 and 18. Results are presented descriptively (mean ± SD of five analytical samples). Compared with the control, the proportion of viable (developing) eggs was lower in the pretreated substrates throughout digestion, most markedly with carvacrol (25.5% vs. 72.8% in the control already on day 3). On day 18, eggs with formed larvae averaged 6.1% in the control and 2.1% and 3.5% in the thymol- and carvacrol-pretreated substrates, respectively. Methane concentration was lower in the pretreated reactors on day 6 but recovered to or above the control level by days 12–18; biogas volume was not quantified. Thymol and carvacrol pretreatment therefore shows potential for improving the parasitological safety of swine manure digestate, which should be confirmed at a larger scale with more replicate reactors, dose optimization and assessment of residual compounds in the digestate.
